method: Targeted reading of exact-version primary PDF abstract, evaluated results, threats and conclusion; physical PDF page numbers are one-indexed. Remaining 14 selected rows are not yet source-screened.

rows.source_locator: PDF p. 9, section 4.9 Threats to Validity; p. 10, section 6 Conclusions and Future Work
rows.source_basis: Badger reports better generated worst-case resource-cost inputs than standalone components, but acknowledges that the hybrid ran one fuzzing plus one symbolic-execution process while each individual baseline ran on one core. Authors explicitly propose parallelizing symbolic execution for a fairer comparison. The source does not report that matched-resource comparison.
rows.candidate_question: At matched total CPU resources, does parallelized Badger generate higher worst-case resource-cost inputs than a standalone cost-guided fuzzer on held-out Java subjects within the same wall-clock budget?
rows.comparison_and_metric: parallelized hybrid versus cost-guided standalone fuzzing; maximum measured resource-cost input per independent Java program at matched CPU budget and wall-clock horizon
rows.falsification_gate: No consistent held-out cost advantage at matched total CPU, or disappearance of the apparent gain when both arms have comparable parallelism, fails the resource-fair benefit claim; a significant advantage in the source's unequal-core setup alone does not count.

rows.source_locator: PDF pp. 1-2 abstract/introduction, pp. 7-8 section 6.5 and section 7 Conclusion
rows.source_basis: The inspected paper states and evaluates its fair streaming submodular-maximization algorithms and hardness results. Its conclusion summarizes completed claims rather than an explicit next open proposition. A stronger ratio or different fairness regime would be reviewer-invented and is not added as a source question.

limitation: Two-paper targeted section screen is not an eligibility prevalence estimate for all 16; the title-only selection is imperfect by design.
